id.description: The unique and required id of this instance.

sourceType.description: The type this view is a presentation of.

label.description:
The default label for instances of this type or a collection of this type within an UI. If not specified, this is
a cleaned-up version of the source type name.

description.description:
The short description of this field, typically used as a tool tip. If unspecified, this is extracted from the
documentation of the source type.

viewFields.description:
The fields declared on the view. This represents the data elements of the source type hierarchy that will be
available with their presentation.

viewActions.description:
The actions declared on the view. This represents the implementation of button/menu items available to the user of
a UI hosted on this view.

title:
A "view" is a metadata object which represents a set of fields and expressions for a single source type.
This is used to efficiently load fields which are needed for a particular user interface presentation.
The view only configures the presentation. The data is managed by the {@link UiModel model}.

Views have a {@link #source source type} and a set of {@link UiViewField fields}. Those fields can add presentation
to the fields of the source type, or they can expose more deeply nested structure by using an expression to produce
the value. See {@link UiViewField#value} for more info.

Views expose {@link UiViewAction actions} which tie logical operations to the UI necessary to invoke them.
These end up invoking type methods, but provide the UI that labels the action and even collects values for the
method arguments.

The data presented by a view comes from a {@link UiModel}. A model is the UI wrapper around an Obj instance,
and it provides abstract operations that allow a general UI to be built that works with any Obj instance.
The other abstraction is the {@link UiCollection} which provides access to a stream of models.

For example, a form control can lay out its fields based on the declarations in the view and interact with Obj
instances through the model. Thus, general-purpose UIs can be built from metadata without knowing the details
of the objects they will be operating on.

@see UiModel
@see UiCollection
@see UiMap
@see TypeDefaultUi
